segments.text: Today, we're going to talk about
something that every medical courier
needs to understand if you want to move
beyond simply getting paid for driving.
We're talking about the financial
difference between routed deliveries and
stat deliveries. And more importantly,
how you can use stat deliveries
strategically while you're already
running a route to increase your overall
revenue. Because there's a big
difference between making money as a
driver and actually thinking like a
business [music] owner. Let's start with
the basics. A scheduled route is
generally about consistency. You have a
defined route, a defined number of
stops, a defined time frame, and usually
a predetermined rate. The advantage of a
route is predictability. You know where
you're going, you have a general idea of
how long you're going to be working, and
you know what you're going to be getting
paid for that commitment. That's
extremely valuable. But there's another
side of the equation, stat work. Stat
deliveries are typically driven by
urgency. The client needs something
moved quickly, and they're willing to
pay for that urgency. That can mean a
higher payout for a single trip compared
with what you might earn from an
individual stop on a scheduled route.
But here's where I want you to think
differently. The goal isn't necessary to
choose between routes and stat work. The
goal is to understand how they can work
together. So, let's say you're already
running a scheduled route. You're
getting paid to be in a particular area,
and you're already putting miles on your
vehicle. Now, imagine a stat request
comes in. And let's say that stat pickup
is only a few miles from where your
route already has you scheduled to be.
That creates an opportunity. You're
already moving, you're already using
your vehicle, you're already spending
time in that general area. So, instead
of looking at that stat as an entirely
separate job, you can start thinking
about how it fits into the route that
you're already running. Now, obviously
there's an important line here. You
cannot compromise the commitments of
that scheduled route just to chase
another payout. If taking the stat
causes you to miss a scheduled pickup or
delivery, you've potentially created a
bigger problem than the extra money it's
worth. But if that stat can be
strategically integrated into your
existing route without compromising your
schedule commitments, now we're talking
about revenue optimization. And this is
where solo couriers need to start
thinking about something beyond the
payout. Think about revenue per mile,
think about revenue per hour, think
about deadhead miles, and think about
what your vehicle's already doing.
Because a $50 stat isn't necessarily a
$50 opportunity. If you have to drive 40
miles out of your way, sit in traffic,
and then drive another 40 miles back to
your route, that payout may not be
nearly as attractive as it looks.
However, if that same stat takes you two
or three miles off your existing route,
brings you right back into the area
you're already working, that's a
completely different financial equation.
You're leveraging miles you're already
going to drive. And that's the mindset
shift I want you to take away from this
video. Don't just look at the payout,
look at the entire trip. Where am I now?
Where am I already scheduled [music] to
go? Where does this stat pick up take
me? Where does it drop me? How much
additional time does it require? How
many additional miles does it create?
And most importantly, does it interfere
with what I've already committed to? If
the answer's no, you've potentially
found a way to increase your revenue
without proportionally increasing your
operating costs. And that can make a
huge difference over the course of a
week, a month, or an entire year. Here's
another concept I want you to
understand, stacking. [music]
You're essentially stacking revenue
opportunities into the same operating
period. You're not trying to cram as
many deliveries as humanly possible into
your day. [music] You're looking for
opportunities that naturally fit
together. Maybe you're heading north on
your route and a stat pickup is also
heading north. Maybe you're already
finishing a delivery near a hospital,
laboratory, or medical facility where
another pickup is available. Maybe your
route has you sitting in a particular
area for 30 minutes before your next
scheduled stop. You have time-sensitive
specimens, supplies, medications,
documents, and other medical materials.
Your responsibility isn't just to make
money. It is to provide reliable service
and excellent patient care. So, stacking
a stat onto your route creates risk.
Don't do it. If it makes you late, don't
do it. If it creates a safety issue,
don't do [music] it. If you're unsure
whether you're authorized to combine
assignments, communicate with dispatch
or the appropriate client contact before
making that decision. Your reputation is
an asset, so protect it. Because one of
the most valuable things you can build
as a medical courier is the reputation
of being dependable. And dependable
doesn't mean saying yes to everything.
It means knowing what you can
realistically handle and executing it
properly. So, here's the strategy I want
you to start thinking about. When you're
running a route, know your route. Know
your stops. Know the general geography.
Know where you have time flexibility.
>> [music]
>> Know where you're going to be throughout
the day. Then, when a stat opportunity
comes in, evaluate it against what
you're already doing. Don't immediately
ask how much does it pay. Ask yourself,
"Where does it take me? How far is it
from where I'm already going? How much
additional time will it take? Does it
create additional deadhead mileage? And
can I complete it without compromising
my existing commitments?" That's how you
start making smarter money decisions.
Because the objective isn't simply to
work harder, it's to make the work
you're already doing more financially
efficient. And that's one of the biggest
differences between simply driving a
vehicle for money and operating a
courier business. You want to understand
your numbers. You want to understand
your routes.
>> [music]
>> You want to understand your costs, and
you want to understand where
opportunities exist to increase revenue
without unnecessarily increasing
expenses or how it might affect patient
care. Several years ago, I owned a
courier company in the Midwest, and we
were short several drivers, so I hopped
in my car to help out. The dispatcher
gave me two stats. One was a title
commitment that was due for [music]
closing on a home. The other was a stat
specimen delivery for one of our lab
clients. Because the title company was a
larger client, the dispatcher wanted me
to complete that delivery before the
specimen delivery. They were both urgent
deliveries, but which one was truly more
important? Well, clearly the specimen
delivery because it involved patient
[music] care. Learn to discern the
difference. So, the next time you're on
a scheduled route and that stat request
comes through, don't automatically say
yes, and don't automatically say no.
Look at the map, look at the clock, look
at your commitments, look at the miles,
look at the payout, and then ask
yourself,
>> [music]
>> "Can I make this stat work within the
route and meet all the time requirements
for both?" That's the mindset. Because
when you learn how to strategically
combine scheduled route revenue with
compatible stat opportunities, you can
start turning the same driving time into
a much more productive revenue day. And
that's how you move from simply being
busy to actually building a more
profitable medical courier business.
Shout out to our members here on
YouTube. Thanks for becoming a member.
We hope you're finding our member-only
content informative and useful. We'll
see you in the next video.

metadata.title: VA Travel Pay Reimbursement
metadata.author: Veterans Health Administration
metadata.shortDescription: VA Travel Pay Reimbursement pays eligible Veterans for mileage and other travel expenses. Learn how to start your travel claims with the Beneficiary Travel Self-Service System.

segments.text: VA Travel Pay Reimbursement
pays eligible Veterans for mileage and other travel
expenses to and from approved health care appointments.
There are two types of travel pay reimbursement for eligible Veterans.
General Health Care Travel and Special Mode Transportation.
The General Health Care Travel benefit covers regular transportation
to include car, plane, train, bus, taxi, or light rail.
To be eligible for the General Health Care Travel benefit,
you must be traveling for care to a VA health care facility
or to a VA approved facility in your community.
You must also meet one of the following conditions:
You're traveling for treatment for a service connected condition.
You receive a VA pension.
Your income is below the maximum annual VA pension rate.
You're traveling for a scheduled VA claim exam,
also called a C and P exam.
You're traveling to get a service dog.
You can't afford to pay for your travel as defined by our guidelines.
Or you have a VA disability rating of 30% or higher.
The Special Mode Transportation benefit includes coverage of special types
of transportation, like an ambulance, ambulette or wheelchair van.
To be eligible for the Special Mode Transportation benefit
you must be traveling for care to a VA health care facility
or to a VA approved facility in your community
and meet all of the following conditions. You're eligible for General Health Car Travel Reimbursement.
A VA health care provider determines that your medical condition
requires an ambulance or a specially equipped van for travel.
And VA has approved your travel in advance, unless the travel is for an emergency
where a delay would threaten your life.
When you're ready to start a claim, simply visit www.VA.gov.
Enter VA travel pay in the search bar and click the top search result
titled VA Travel Pay Reimbursement.
Here you will find detailed instructions and all of the information
you need to file your travel claim. If you need help.
Scroll down
until you see the heading that reads What if I need help submitting my claim?
Then follow that link to find the travel contact for your facility.
For additional help,
contact the Beneficiary Travel Self-Service System Toll-Free Call Center.

Medical courier insurance, commercial auto insurance, cargo van insurance, and pharmacy delivery insurance are some of the most misunderstood topics in the delivery business. In this video, I break down the differences between personal and commercial insurance, why cargo van insurance costs more, how local courier routes affect your risk profile, and one of the biggest mistakes new drivers make when talking to insurance companies.

If you're starting a medical courier business, pharmacy delivery service, hospital discharge support business, or local logistics company, this video will help you better understand how insurance companies view your operation and why the way you describe your business matters.

Whether you're using a sedan, SUV, minivan, Transit Connect, or Sprinter van, understanding insurance is critical before taking on contracts and growing your business.

metadata.shortDescription:
Looking for medical courier jobs with no experience in 2026? Discover 4 medical courier companies to research, independent contractor opportunities, vehicle requirements, insurance, and how beginners can get started.

If you've been searching for entry-level medical courier jobs but keep running into companies requiring previous experience, commercial insurance, HIPAA training, or certifications, this video is for you.

Today on Giganomic Era, we're breaking down OnWay Transport, Lab Logistics, Medical Delivery Services (MDS), and carGO Health to help you understand which companies may consider beginners and what you need before applying.

Whether you drive a sedan, SUV, or cargo van, you'll learn how to research medical courier opportunities that match your vehicle, schedule, and location.

00:00 Medical Courier Jobs With No Experience
01:00 OnWay Transport — Beginner Courier Opportunities
03:25 Lab Logistics — Medical Courier Driver Applications
04:55 Medical Delivery Services (MDS) — Dedicated Routes
06:45 carGO Health — Training and Onboarding
08:15 Medical Courier Certifications and Training
08:45 Auto Insurance Requirements for Medical Couriers
09:50 How to Apply Without Medical Courier Experience
11:00 Finding Your First Medical Courier Opportunity

🚗 4 MEDICAL COURIER COMPANIES TO CHECK OUT

1. OnWay Transport
Medical courier opportunities involving pharmacies, hospitals, laboratories, STAT deliveries, and scheduled routes. No previous medical courier experience required according to its driver information.

Website: https://www.onway.com/drive/

2. Lab Logistics
Medical courier services across the United States. Submit your driver profile to be considered for opportunities in your area. Previous courier experience may be preferred rather than required for certain openings.

Website: https://www.lablogistics.com/drive-for-us

3. Medical Delivery Services (MDS)
Independent contractor opportunities involving dedicated medical delivery routes, with vehicle, insurance, and background-check requirements that vary by position.

Website: https://www.medicaldeliveryservices.com/

4. carGO Health
Healthcare courier opportunities with structured onboarding, medical courier training, and driver shadowing. Acceptance depends on applicant qualifications and available openings.

Website: https://www.cargo.health/careers/

Subscribe to Giganomic Era for medical courier jobs, pharmacy delivery opportunities, independent contractor routes, courier business pricing, insurance information, and strategies for building your own direct-client courier business.

#MedicalCourierJobs #MedicalCourier #NoExperienceJobs #IndependentContractor #CourierBusiness

Subscribe to our channel for more NMT
content. All businesses across all
industries face the risk of frauds.
Detecting fraud can be quite
challenging. It requires a thorough
analysis of all data transactions and
comparing them to known models of fraud.
State governments and private companies
are constantly reviewing ways to reduce
the risk of fraud. These can have a
dangerous effect on passengers and
patients, especially those who need
efficient services for medical
treatments. This guide outlines tips to
overcome all kinds of fraudulent
activities in NMT services. Medical
transportation fraud. Transport
providers are required to meet federal
and state regulations. Unfortunately,
many transport service companies have
seen integrity concerns rise in recent
years. This is mainly due to fraudulent
billing activities and patient safety.
NMT companies usually work with
passengers who are covered by Medicaid.
Since states are required to provide
NAMT services to beneficiaries, they
have set up some regulations for
transport providers. But they also have
considerable discretion in delivering
their services. As a result, [music]
providers have different ways of
providing for their passengers needs.
Some work directly with state
transportation departments while others
partner with brokers or manage care
organizations MCOs. Given this wide
range of services and the gaps in
Medicaid data systems, it is essential
to have measures in place to prevent
fraud in NMT.
Types of fraud common in NMT. Providers
experience several types of fraud when
they work with all kinds of healthcare
providers and facilities and that
includes government MAMT programs. Here
are some of the most common ones.
Improper billing. These issues in the
NAMT industry include billing for
services not rendered, additional fees
for undisclosed items, and client claims
after payment has been submitted to
other providers. Medicaid eligibility.
[snorts] Some providers face fraud when
it comes to the eligibility of a patient
for Medicare or Medicaid programs. Many
NEMT companies do not require prior
approval before providing standard
services to passengers. The priority is
bringing patients where they need to go.
State regulations require that some NAMT
services require prior approval,
especially when it requires extended
service hours, trips that exceed the
maximum mileage, and trips that require
lodging, food, or unusual transportation
modes such as air ambulances. Many NMT
providers find that some passengers are
not eligible for such services and the
trip remains unpaid due to a lack of
approval at the state level. Fraudulent
credentials. Many states require
specific certifications and permits for
an NAM service provider to operate.
However, some states are not strict
enough with these regulations, resulting
in many transport providers that lack
first aid certifications, vehicle and
driver permits and licenses, or even
staff with criminal backgrounds. Some
drivers also declare they completed a
service or trip even though they did not
pick up any passenger. When they make
these claims, they can receive payment
for services they did not render.
Additionally, if a driver does not have
the training to provide medical aid,
this puts the safety of the passengers
at considerable risk. If a passenger
suddenly requires medical attention in
the middle of a trip, they will not get
the help they need. Unauthorized rides.
Another form of fraud is passengers
taking unauthorized rides. Most NMT
companies receive only a name, a contact
number, and a pickup point. Some
passengers take advantage of this and
use fake identities to receive transport
services. Often these passengers use
their Medicaid or Medicare privilege to
take trips unrelated to medical
treatments or therapies. They book a
subsidized trip ostensibly for a checkup
and then go somewhere else like a movie
theater or grocery store. Some even pass
on the discounted trip to another
person. Sometimes drivers and passengers
partner up to defraud transport
companies through NMT ghost rides. The
passenger schedules a long-distance trip
and the driver picks them up. However,
they do not go to their destination and
instead share the profits. Tips to
prevent and detect NAMT transport fraud
The industry is facing significant
challenge in avoiding and overcoming
instances of fraud. They are a drain on
resources and waste efforts to provide
help to those who truly need medical
assistance. Dealing with fraud requires
a combination of technology and human
persistence. Preventing improper
billing. One way for a service provider
to control improper billing is to
leverage robust NMT software to ensure
[music] that each transaction is
certified and completed. They can review
each passenger, the service provided,
and the hours or miles of the trip.
Billing systems can also verify the
eligibility of a passenger to a state
Medicaid [music] program, which reduces

metadata.title: Congress Wants Every Medicaid Trip Verified? Genie Journal Recap, NEMT News October 2026
metadata.author: RouteGenie
metadata.shortDescription:
A bill in Congress would require electronic proof of every Medicaid trip starting January 2027. Three states moved on coverage, contracts, and rural funding. And a Mayo Clinic study finally put a number on what a missing ride costs.

October was the month the trip became the thing everyone is measuring. Here's what it means for transportation providers, brokers, and health plans.

RouteGenie builds routing, dispatching, billing, and credentialing software for NEMT providers. 

See how it works:

📞 1 (877) 599-6560

Follow us on social: 
Facebook: https://www.facebook.com/routegenie/
LinkedIn: https://www.linkedin.com/company/routegenie/
Twitter: https://twitter.com/theroutegenie
Instagram: https://www.instagram.com/routegenie/

━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━

TIMECODES

0:00 — October in 20 seconds
0:21 — Welcome to the Genie Journal Recap
0:41 — HR 10618: the STOP Medicaid Fraud Act and six-point trip verification
1:36 — Iowa proposes NEMT coverage for low-income adults as CMS ends the waiver
2:13 — Louisiana opens its statewide fee-for-service broker contract to bids
2:36 — Kansas grants target the rural transportation gap
3:14 — CMS launches Investing in Health Outcomes with 37 state partners
4:07 — Mayo Clinic: unmet transportation needs cut show rates by 5.2 points
4:46 — Minnesota ties NEMT mileage rates to fuel prices — and raises them
5:31 — RouteGenie: the trips your fleet can't take
5:58 — The question October asked every provider

━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━

THE NUMBERS

• 6 data points per trip under the proposed federal verification standard
• January 1, 2027 — proposed compliance date, and the date Iowa's waiver ends
• November 24 — Louisiana broker proposals due
• November 18 — Kansas grant applications close
• 37 founding state partners in the CMS outcomes model
• ~450 reporting requirements across 42 states, most of them process-based
• 859,346 primary care visits analyzed by Mayo Clinic across 5 states
• 5.2 percentage points — the drop in show rates tied to unmet transportation needs
• $1.92 per loaded wheelchair mile in Minnesota, up from $1.76 in April
• $2.71 per loaded stretcher mile, up from $2.49

moved from a broker requirement to a

electronic verification for Medicaid
non-emergency transportation from
January 1st, 2027.

the service, who received it, who
provided it, the date, the location, and
when it began and ended.
This is a proposal, not law and most
introduced bills never move.
But look at those six data points. A GPS
equipped dispatch system records them on
every trip already.
And many broker contracts have required
them for years.
Providers whose records carry all six
are starting from the right place.
Washington wants proof of the trip.
Three states spent October creating more
trips to prove.
Iowa's Department of Health and Human
Services proposed adding non-emergency
transportation for the Iowa Health and
Wellness Plan. It's Medicaid coverage
for low-income adults.
Iowa had waived rides for that group and
CMS will not renew the waiver after
January 1st, 2027 [music].
If approved, that is new covered trip
volume arriving on one date. And Iowa
providers have one quarter to talk
capacity [music] with their managed care
plans.
Further south, a whole state program is
up for bid.
On October 15th, the Louisiana Division
of Administration opened bidding for a
broker to run Medicaid fee-for-service
transportation statewide, with proposals
due November 24th.
A new broker means a new network, and
every provider in the state gets a fresh
look.
And in Kansas, the money is going
straight to the rural gap.
On October 16th, the Kansas Department
of Health and Environment opened grants
for sustainable transportation that gets
rural residents to medical appointments.
Applications close November 18th.
Amounts are pending CMS approval, and
the grants [music] cannot replace
services Medicaid already reimburses.
That last rule is the opportunity.
The money is for what does not exist
yet.
New routes, new partnerships, new
service models in counties where the
nearest clinic is an hour away.
Those trips are also being measured
differently, and October brought both
the policy and the evidence.
On September 25th, CMS launched
investing in health outcomes with 37
founding state [music] partners.
Moving Medicaid quality measurement away
from paperwork and toward results in
prevention, chronic disease, and
behavioral health.
A CMS analysis [music] had found roughly
450 reporting requirements across 42
states, most of them about process.
States that sign commit to outcome
targets and to building those measures
into upcoming procurements.
Dialysis adherence, diabetes control,
and behavioral health engagement all
depend on the ride showing up.
A provider who can show a health plan
completed [music] trip and on-time rates
is speaking the language the plan is now
measured in.
And the research backs the policy.
A Mayo Clinic study [music] in the
Journal of General Internal Medicine
looked at more than 859,000 in-person
primary care visits across five states
[music].
Patients with unmet transportation needs
were 5.2 percentage points less likely
to show up.
A larger effect than [music] food
insecurity,
housing instability, or financial
strain.
Virtual visits showed no difference.
That is the figure to bring to a health
plan meeting.
The ride is a measurable lever. And now
there is a number on it.
Proving the trip and measuring it.
One state spent October paying for it.
Minnesota raised its state-administered
NEMT mileage rates on October 1st
[music] under a fuel formula written
into state law.
Wheelchair mileage now pays $1.92 per
loaded mile.
It paid $1.76 in April.
Stretcher mileage pays $2.71 [music]
after $2.49.
The rate moves with fuel prices every
quarter automatically.
Minnesota's [music] formula is one any
state or broker can copy.
And providers negotiating anywhere else
can put it on the table.
The argument isn't margin. It's whether
the ride shows up.
One thing from us this month.
A new guide on the RouteGenie blog
covers the trips your fleet can't take.
Rideshare adds a fourth choice beyond
declining, subcontracting, or
reshuffling.
A passenger car for ambulatory [music]
trips sent from your own dispatch screen
while your fleet keeps everything
[music] else.
The guide shows how one integration
handles it in practice.
That's it for this month's Genie Journal
recap.
October asked every provider one
question. Can you prove the trip
happened and what was it worth?
The ones who can answer are who every
new contract is looking for.
Like and subscribe so you don't miss
[music] the next recap.
See you next month.

metadata.shortDescription:
Fraud charges, grant money, and a broker shakeup. Here is what mattered in medical transportation in August 2026, and what it means for NEMT providers.

Subscribe to The Genie Journal newsletter: https://go.routegenie.com/newsletter

CHAPTERS
00:00 Intro
00:19 RouteGenie at NEMTAC Transform 2026
01:13 DOJ charges the "War Room" in a $12M Medicaid transportation fraud case
03:04 Alabama, West Virginia and North Dakota put $8.5M behind NEMT capacity
04:40 A 125-mile wheelchair trip to the Wisconsin Capitol
05:47 Modivcare wins Maine and takes over Montana NEMT
07:03 Nevada approves robotaxi permits for Tesla, Waymo and Uber
08:23 RouteGenie now integrates with Uber Health
08:52 Inside the Lamp with BraunAbility, plus the SourceForge Podcast
09:35 What August rewarded

IN THIS EPISODE
Prosecutors say an outside operation manufactured ride data and spoofed GPS coordinates, then supplied it to companies that billed Medicaid. The claims were caught as "unmatched," with no medical visit ever billed against them. Meanwhile Rural Health Transformation dollars landed in three states specifically for vehicles, wheelchair-accessible capacity, and discharge transportation. Modivcare secured its MaineCare contract in court and picks up Montana on October first, which makes enrollment with the incoming broker time-sensitive in both states. Plus a new Inside the Lamp episode: Cameron Craig talks with Jake Craig and John Maselli of BraunAbility about choosing the right vehicle for NEMT, what ADA compliance actually requires, minivan supply, electric and autonomous vehicles, and the wheelchair securement problem nobody in the AV conversation is solving.

only and does not constitute legal,

The NMT compliance checklist. Five legal
essentials for business success. Welcome
to Route Genie community. If you want
smarter, easier, and more profitable
ways to run your NEMt business, hit like
and subscribe and let's dive in.
Starting an NMT business means entering
a highly regulated industry. While
states are legally required to provide
medical transportation for Medicaid
beneficiaries, they often rely on
private operators to fill the gaps, that
opportunity comes with serious legal
responsibilities.
Why NMT regulations exist? NMT providers
serve vulnerable populations, the sick,
elderly, and people with disabilities.
These passengers require special care.
Their transportation involves
significant legal liability. Plus, when
you're receiving state subsidies,
compliance isn't optional. Understanding
these regulations isn't just about
avoiding penalties. It's about building
credibility and trust within the health
care system while protecting your
business from costly mistakes. The five
essential compliance areas. One,
certification and licensing
requirements. Every state has different
Medicaid programs and NMT regulations.
You'll need to check with your local
health services department for specific
licenses and certifications required for
your business and employees. Standard
requirements typically include business
licenses, insurance approvals, and
driver specific certifications like CDL
endorsements or CPR training. The key is
understanding both state and federal
guidelines and maintaining clear records
of all necessary licenses.
Two, HIPPA compliance. Since NAMT
providers handle sensitive patient
information related to appointments and
care needs, HIPPA compliance is
mandatory. This federal law protects
patients protected health information.
Your compliance strategy should include
secure handling of patient details,
HIPPA compliant software with encryption
and access controls, comprehensive staff
training on patient data handling, and
robust security protocols, including
password management and regular audits.
NMT software like Route Genie can help
maintain HIPPA standards while providing
automated routing, dispatch, and
scheduling features. The platform also
includes client and driver apps for
seamless communication, billing, and
payment processing.
Three, vehicle compliance and driver
requirements. Most NAMT passengers have
mobility challenges, so ADA compliance
becomes legally required when your
business scales to over 15 employees.
Requirements vary by state, but
generally focus on door dimensions,
safety equipment, and accessibility
hardware. NMT fleets typically use
modified minivans and full-size vans
equipped for accessibility, safety, and
passenger comfort. You may also need
durable medical equipment like mobility
aids, respiratory care devices, and
monitoring equipment for specialized
trips. Driver requirements are equally
strict. Most states require specialized
training for assisting passengers with
special needs, physical examinations to
ensure fitness for duty, drug testing
with zero tolerance for substance abuse,
and extensive background checks covering
criminal records and behavioral issues.
Four, Medicaid billing compliance. The
majority of NMT users are Medicaid
beneficiaries, so you must adhere to
strict billing standards set by CMS and
state Medicaid agencies. This includes
using correct billing codes, maintaining
detailed trip documentation, and
implementing fraudrevention measures.
Proper Medicaid billing ensures timely
reimbursements, helps avoid legal
complications, and builds trust with
state health agencies. Getting this
wrong can result in payment delays,
audits, and potential legal issues.
Five, insurance and liability coverage.
Comprehensive insurance isn't just
legally required. It's critical for
business survival. Essential policies
include general liability, commercial
auto liability, professional liability
for errors and omissions, workers
compensation, and umbrella coverage for
larger claims. Working with an NMT savvy
insurance adviser helps tailor policies
to your specific service needs while
ensuring you meet all legal

Five legal essentials for business success. Welcome to Route Genie community. If you want smarter, easier, and more profitable ways to run your NEMt business, hit like and subscribe and let's dive in. Starting an NMT business means entering a highly regulated industry. While states are legally required to provide medical transportation for Medicaid beneficiaries, they often rely on private operators to fill the gaps, that opportunity comes with serious legal responsibilities. Why NMT regulations exist? NMT providers serve vulnerable populations, the sick, elderly, and people with disabilities. These passengers require special care. Their transportation involves significant legal liability. Plus, when you're receiving state subsidies, compliance isn't optional. Understanding these regulations isn't just about avoiding penalties. It's about building credibility and trust within the health care system while protecting your business from costly mistakes. The five essential compliance areas. One, certification and licensing requirements. Every state has different Medicaid programs and NMT regulations. You'll need to check with your local health services department for specific licenses and certifications required for your business and employees. Standard requirements typically include business licenses, insurance approvals, and driver specific certifications like CDL endorsements or CPR training. The key is understanding both state and federal guidelines and maintaining clear records of all necessary licenses. Two, HIPPA compliance. Since NAMT providers handle sensitive patient information related to appointments and care needs, HIPPA compliance is mandatory. This federal law protects patients protected health information. Your compliance strategy should include secure handling of patient details, HIPPA compliant software with encryption and access controls, comprehensive staff training on patient data handling, and robust security protocols, including password management and regular audits. NMT software like Route Genie can help maintain HIPPA standards while providing automated routing, dispatch, and scheduling features. The platform also includes client and driver apps for seamless communication, billing, and payment processing. Three, vehicle compliance and driver requirements. Most NAMT passengers have mobility challenges, so ADA compliance becomes legally required when your business scales to over 15 employees. Requirements vary by state, but generally focus on door dimensions, safety equipment, and accessibility hardware. NMT fleets typically use modified minivans and full-size vans equipped for accessibility, safety, and passenger comfort. You may also need durable medical equipment like mobility aids, respiratory care devices, and monitoring equipment for specialized trips. Driver requirements are equally strict. Most states require specialized training for assisting passengers with special needs, physical examinations to ensure fitness for duty, drug testing with zero tolerance for substance abuse, and extensive background checks covering criminal records and behavioral issues. Four, Medicaid billing compliance. The majority of NMT users are Medicaid beneficiaries, so you must adhere to strict billing standards set by CMS and state Medicaid agencies. This includes using correct billing codes, maintaining detailed trip documentation, and implementing fraudrevention measures. Proper Medicaid billing ensures timely reimbursements, helps avoid legal complications, and builds trust with state health agencies. Getting this wrong can result in payment delays, audits, and potential legal issues. Five, insurance and liability coverage. Comprehensive insurance isn't just legally required. It's critical for business survival. Essential policies include general liability, commercial auto liability, professional liability for errors and omissions, workers compensation, and umbrella coverage for larger claims. Working with an NMT savvy insurance adviser helps tailor policies to your specific service needs while ensuring you meet all legal requirements. Staying current with regulations. Compliance isn't a one-time setup. Laws change constantly, so you need reliable information sources. Government websites like CMS provide regular updates on Medicaid policies and guidelines, while the Department of Transportation offers vehicle standards and regulations. State specific resources through your local Medicaid or Department of Health websites provide updates on regional requirements. Industry associations like the non-emergency medical transportation accreditation commission offer standards, certification processes, and regulatory guidance. Specialized resources such as the HIPPA journal help providers stay current on healthcare data protection requirements. Technology as your compliance partner. Modern NMT software doesn't just streamline operations. It helps maintain compliance across multiple areas from HIPPA compliant data handling to automated billing and documentation. The right technology platform reduces compliance risks while improving service quality. The bottom line business success depends heavily on compliance and service excellence. While the regulatory landscape may seem overwhelming, understanding these five core areas provide your foundation for safe, legal, and profitable operations. metadata.shortDescription:
NEMT audits are getting tighter, and an email won't protect you anymore. In this episode, That NEMT Girl (Teya Miles) sits down with Amanda Lynn from Zeit Ride to talk about how small non-emergency medical transportation providers can prove every trip, avoid costly audit losses, and scale from 1 to 5 to 10+ vehicles.

Teya has been in the NEMT industry for 7 years and has been audited herself. She shares the real story of a canceled appointment that almost cost her company two rides, why Medicaid is auditing with "binoculars" now, and why she's warning providers about July of next year.

In this video you'll learn:
✅ Why "he say, she say" doesn't hold up in a Medicaid audit
✅ How one month of missing trip proof can cost you $12,000–$15,000
✅ How NEMT dispatch software saves hours on routing and scheduling
✅ Why sending the wrong vehicle (wheelchair, bariatric) costs you money and trust
✅ How dash cams and trip records protect your revenue
✅ What Zeit Ride costs ($50 per vehicle per month) and who it's built for

Whether you're a new NEMT provider still driving, dispatching, and answering calls yourself, or you're ready to grow your fleet, this conversation gives you the real.

metadata.title: GPS with NEMT
metadata.author: SwiftAid Transport
metadata.shortDescription:
In this episode of AI – The Deep Dive for SwiftAid, two AI hosts examine how GPS (Global Positioning System) software plays a critical role in securing, monitoring, and improving Non-Emergency Medical Transportation (NEMT).


Medical transportation depends on more than just vehicles and drivers—it relies on real-time visibility, accurate tracking, and verifiable data. One AI host explains how GPS technology enables transportation providers to monitor vehicle locations, optimize routes, confirm pickups and drop-offs, and maintain accurate trip records. The discussion highlights how these capabilities contribute to operational efficiency, accountability, and improved coordination with healthcare facilities.


The second AI host challenges the topic by asking the questions listeners may be thinking: How does GPS tracking actually improve patient safety? Can it prevent fraud or misuse within transportation systems? What happens when tracking data is incomplete, inaccurate, or not properly utilized? And how does real-time visibility affect trust between patients, providers, and transportation companies?


Using research-based insights, the episode explores how GPS software supports transparency by creating a digital record of each trip. This includes timestamps, route verification, and real-time updates that can be shared with dispatch teams, healthcare facilities, and, in some cases, patients or family members. The conversation also examines how GPS systems can help reduce disputes, improve scheduling accuracy, and provide data-driven insights for continuous improvement.


Rather than presenting GPS as a simple navigation tool, this episode positions it as a core component of a secure and accountable transportation system. When integrated properly with dispatch and scheduling platforms, GPS technology becomes part of a larger ecosystem that supports reliability, compliance, and operational oversight.


SwiftAid Transport is referenced as a case study in how transportation providers can leverage GPS-driven systems to enhance transparency, reduce uncertainty, and build trust through verifiable data and structured workflows.


All audio in this episode is fully generated using artificial intelligence. The dialogue is designed to be analytical, transparent, and educational, offering listeners a deeper understanding of how technology supports safer and more reliable medical transportation.


This episode continues the series’ mission to elevate the conversation around Non-Emergency Medical Transportation by examining how tools, systems, and data-driven approaches contribute to better outcomes for patients, providers, and transportation teams.

non-emergency medical transportation
billing software to keep track of all
the parameters surrounding deadhead
miles.
To properly understand how to set a
pricing structure and how to charge for
deadhead miles, it is necessary to know
what deadhead miles are and when they
should be applied to a trip.
What are deadhead miles?
The best way to explain deadhead miles
is through a hypothetical scenario.
Let's take a look at NEMT company ABC
Transport.
ABC Transport is located in the center
of a major city.
John Smith is wheelchair bound and needs
transport to a doctor's office in the
major city but lives 40 miles outside of
this major city.
ABC Transport is the selected company
for this trip.
When we look at the scenario above,
there are two legs to the trip.
Taking John Smith from his home to the
doctor's office and from the doctor's
office back home. In reality, for the
transportation company, there are four
legs.
ABC Transport has to send a driver 40
miles just to pick up John Smith and
when John Smith is dropped back off at
his home, the driver has to travel 40
miles back to the city.
There is no client in the vehicle for
this portion of the trip but the miles
driven pertain to the trip. These are
the deadhead miles.
Pricing structure.
So, the question still remains, how do
you charge for the deadhead miles?
The answer can vary between different
companies.
But if you have NEMT dispatch and
billing software to keep track of
pricing and when deadhead miles apply,

the central location where your services
are provided. Trips originating outside
of this radius or traveling somewhere
outside of this radius should have a
deadhead mileage charge included.
If ABC Transport had a 25-mile radius,
they would be charging for 15 deadhead
miles each way for John Smith's trip.
The price per mile is up to you.
With the right kind of NEMT billing
software, it should be as simple as
plugging these numbers in and letting
the software do all of the thinking and
calculating.

segments.text: How to justify your NEMT rates.
We want to share our NEMT content with
you on a regular basis. Subscribe to our
channel so you never miss a video. The
non-emergency medical transport NEMT
industry is highly regulated and the
government has mandated specific
guidelines for providers and third-party
payers. In order to justify the rates
being charged by NEMT providers, it is
essential to consider the factors that
go into setting them. Business owners
are aware of the impact their rates have
on their clients and the industry as a
whole.
NEMT rates matter for three key reasons.
They impact the quality of care patients
receive, influence the sustainability of
NEMT providers, and set the standards
for all other businesses. Let's take a
closer look. Why NEMT rates matter. NEMT
rates impact the quality of care
patients receive. In the United States,
NEMT rates are set by individual
business owners based on the
recommendations set by the NTD Uniform
System of Accounts (USOA). This can lead
to a patchwork of specific rates across
the country impacting the quality of
care patients receive.
Some states have very high rates, which
allows providers to offer a higher level
of care. Other states have lower rates,
which may lead to service limitations
such as distance and scheduling. All
providers are obliged to meet industry
requirements and regulations, but if
they have limited resources, some NEMT
companies may only cater to specific
clients or passengers and may not be
able to cover patients with high-level
needs. This also means that the
reimbursement rate for providers could
trend even lower. The lack of revenue in
a particular area can lead to
consolidation and a decrease in the
number of providers available to provide
services for patients.
NEMT rates influence the sustainability
of NEMT providers. Medicaid NEMT rates
vary considerably and this variation
significantly impacts the sustainability
of NEMT as a whole. In general, Medicaid
programs reimburse NEMT providers at
lower rates than private payers. The
difference between Medicaid and private
payer rates is even greater for trips
that are longer or involve more complex
care.
This variation in reimbursement rates
creates a financial challenge for NEMT
providers who must often choose between
providing care at a loss or limiting the
number and type of services they offer.
As a result, many NEMT providers are not
able to offer a full range of services
or serve all Medicaid eligible clients.
This limits access to care for Medicaid
beneficiaries and can lead to poorer
health outcomes for many patients.
NEMT rates set the standard for the
industry. Non-medical transportation
rates are set to ensure that patients
have access to the care they need when
they need it. This ensures that
providers can offer these services at a
fair price for both parties.
Interstate NEMT rates. For many NEMT
providers, the average rate will vary in
every state, but most of it depends on a
broker. Non-emergency medical
transportation rates in California may
differ from non-emergency medical
transportation rates in Texas.
Aside from considering the operational
costs and wage rates in each state, the
rates can be determined in two ways
across the country. Setting a rate
floor. A rate floor is a minimum rate
that a provider must be paid for their
service. Providers can negotiate the
rate floor with their broker, especially
if it results in a deficit. Direct
negotiations.
Some states allow providers to set a
minimum rate, which means allowing the
medical care organization and broker to
negotiate for each provider. This
ensures that the provider can charge a
fair fee for everyone involved. Aside
from these, fuel costs, the demand for
NEMT services in the area, and the level
of service provided are also considered.
NEMT transportation rates. As the NEMT
industry continues to grow, transport
businesses need to remain competitive by
offering affordable rates. NEMT rates
are determined by many factors,
especially when the trip is not covered
by insurance. These include the type of
service being provided, the distance
traveled, and the number of passengers.
While it may be tempting to cut rates or
reduce costs to attract more customers,
this can harm your business. If you
charge too little, you may not be able
to cover your cost or generate profit.
This can lead to many serious problems
down the road, and it can also hurt the
industry as a whole by driving down
prices. Charging a fair price ensures
the longevity of a business as well as
the quality and variety of services on
offer.
Establishing competitive and sustainable
pricing for an NEMT business is a
crucial element of success. Your prices
must cover the cost of providing
services and maintain a healthy profit
margin.
When setting rates for your NEMT
service, the USOA recommends several
points.
Cost of operating your business,
including vehicle maintenance, fuel, and
driver salaries. Demand for transport
services in your area.
Price of similar services in your area.
Tax rates in your area. Additional
expenses, utilities, supplies, and
indirect costs. Insurance.
Depreciation. Miscellaneous expenses.
Once you've added up all of these
elements, you can begin in calculating
and establishing pricing for your NEMT
business.
Review your prices periodically to
ensure they are still competitive and in
line with the cost of running your
business and the overall industry
average rate. How to set rates for your
NEMT service.
NEMT rates are based on the average cost
of providing services to patients. These
rates ensure that transportation
companies offer a fair and reasonable
price as they generate a healthy profit
margin.
If you want to start an NEMT business,
here's how you can set the rates for
your services.
Know the demand. The first thing you
should know about your clientele is the
type of service they need and the kind
of insurance coverage they have. You
must understand the level of demand of
your target audience and begin
calculating costs from there. You can
also research the average market rate in
the area for the services you aim to
provide. These metrics will help you
arrive at a reasonable price.
Consider your operational costs. Aside
from vehicle maintenance, fuel expenses,
and driver salaries, you must also
consider other operational expenses such
as insurance, management software,
licenses, permits, and more. You can
then set a base rate that covers all of
these costs plus a reasonable profit
margin.
Include additional fees.
Additional fees may cover expenses for
extra miles, time, or even scheduling
that would require additional pay for
your drivers or personnel.
You could charge the following fees:
weekend rates, holiday rates, additional
distance rate, charge per mile, no-show
fees, late fees, special trips, deadhead
miles.
Late fees can be charged per hour or
depending on your base rate. For no-show
fees, you can set a rate that will cover
the inconvenience for your staff and
driver for the scheduling. You can
reduce no-shows for your NEMT business
by using scheduling software that
reminds passengers of an upcoming trip.
The price for special trips depend on
the number of passengers, distance, the
type of equipment needed, and even the
time of day.
Some transport companies also charge for
deadhead miles, which include the
mileage covered without the passenger in
the vehicle. This applies to passengers
who may live farther than the company's
usual coverage and will require more
time and fuel to get picked up. Create a
structure for billing.
You must break down how you will charge
for your services. Creating a billing
structure that accounts for all of the
charges and fees involved will give your
passengers clarity and understanding of
what they're paying for and the value of
your service.
Include the following: load fee. This is
the initial charge for the pickup, and
it can vary depending on the vehicle and
service type. Minimum charge flat rate.
This can be implemented for
short-distance two and fro trips. A flat
rate can also be implemented for clients
that require frequent trips. Per mile
rate. This is added to initial charges,
load fees, and minimum charges,
especially for medical transportation
long-distance trips. Holiday, weekend,
after-hours rate. These rates can be
added for weekends, holidays, or
after-hours schedules. If your business
runs 24/7 operations, you can apply a
surcharge for late-night and early
morning trips.
Final thoughts. NEMT providers are
businesses that provide a vital service
to the healthcare system, and they need
to charge rates that are high enough to
cover their costs and generate a profit.
Rates in the NEMT industry are set based
on the complex cost of providing a
variety of high-quality services that
help passengers, patients, and medical
organizations. To give your clients the
clarity they need to understand your
rates, your NEMT business must use the
right tools and software to manage your
billing structure. RouteGenie automates
the billing process from start to
finish, which increases your clean claim
rate and reduces time spent on billing,
all while allowing for faster
reimbursement times and overall
productivity. Book a demo today. Don't
postpone your growth till tomorrow. We
hope you enjoyed this video. If you did,
please like it and subscribe for more
great NEMT content.

🚨🏥 NEW MEDICAL COURIERS! DO YOU KNOW WHAT SUPPLIES YOU NEED BEFORE YOUR FIRST DELIVERY? 🚗📦

When I onboarded with RAPID MEDICAL, they sent me supplies to help prepare for my assignments!

💡 THIS IS WHY IT’S IMPORTANT TO PROVIDE YOUR CORRECT MAILING ADDRESS DURING ONBOARDING!

Some courier companies provide equipment, uniforms, and supplies, while others require you to purchase approved items yourself.

📦 ESSENTIAL MEDICAL COURIER SUPPLIES TO KNOW ABOUT:

✅ Biohazard specimen bags — For properly packaged specimens when required.

✅ Insulated transport bags — For temperature-sensitive deliveries.

✅ Reusable ice packs or gel packs — For shipments requiring approved cold packaging.

✅ Hard-sided transport containers — For secure specimen transportation.

✅ Disposable gloves and PPE — When required for the assignment.

✅ Spill response kit — For trained personnel handling applicable specimen shipments.

✅ Temperature monitoring devices — When required for cold-chain deliveries.

✅ Hand sanitizer and disinfecting supplies — For appropriate hygiene and cleaning.

✅ Safety vest, ID badge, and uniform — Depending on company requirements.

✅ Phone charger and delivery tracking app — For communication and proof of delivery.

🛒 WHERE CAN YOU GET SUPPLIES?

You can research approved supplies online or at medical supply stores and other retailers.

🔗 I’LL INCLUDE A LINK TO SUPPLIES!

⚠️ IMPORTANT: Don’t purchase everything before onboarding! Ask your courier company what they provide and which equipment is approved. Medical shipments have specific packaging, handling, and temperature requirements.

🔥 MY ADVICE: GET PREPARED, STAY ORGANIZED, AND FOLLOW YOUR COMPANY’S TRANSPORTATION PROCEDURES!

In this medical courier ride-along, I'm taking you with me for 3 pharmacy deliveries and a medical supply run involving 3 oxygen tanks — but the real lesson is how I price the work.

My normal pharmacy delivery rate is $45 per pickup and delivery within 20 miles, but when this pharmacy gives me multiple orders at the same time, my rate drops to $35 per delivery. Why would I accept less per delivery? Because volume, mileage, time, route efficiency and recurring work all matter when pricing courier contracts.

I also show you another side of healthcare logistics that many new independent medical couriers overlook medical supply delivery and reverse logistics. Healthcare businesses don't just need items delivered — equipment, supplies and medical devices also need to be picked up, returned and exchanged.

In this video, we talk about:
• Medical courier pricing and courier rates
• Pharmacy delivery contracts
• When volume discounts make sense
• Per-delivery vs. hourly and route pricing
• Medical supply and equipment delivery
• Reverse logistics opportunities
• Building direct medical courier contracts
• Recurring clients vs. depending on delivery apps
• Questions to ask before quoting a courier job
• How to protect your time and profit

If you're trying to start a medical courier business, become an independent medical courier, get pharmacy delivery contracts, find direct courier clients, or learn how to price medical delivery services, this is the side of the business you need to understand.

Don't just ask, “What should I charge per delivery?”

Ask: What does the entire job require, and is the relationship profitable?

Subscribe to Gigonomics for more real-world medical courier, pharmacy delivery, healthcare logistics, senior service and direct-contract business strategies.

🚀 NEED HELP BUILDING YOUR COURIER BUSINESS?

If you're serious about starting or growing your medical courier business and need help with pricing, finding direct clients, outreach, contracts, insurance, or putting the business together, I offer 1-on-1 coaching where we work on YOUR business and YOUR market.

 want you to search federal contract databases (like FPDS, USAspending.gov, or SAM.gov) for medical courier / delivery contracts (PSC code R602) that are available or recently awarded in the area of [INSERT YOUR CITY OR STATE HERE].

offers drug testing methods on a broad range of sample types including urine oral fluid and hair
each method has its advantages and disadvantages this tutorial will help you compare them and
will help you determine which type or types best match your company's objectives for a lab-based
urine collection the sample is collected in a securely sealed specimen cup and is shipped to
an accredited analytical laboratory for testing as the gold standard model for workplace drug testing
in north america this is the only acceptable sample type for employers who are regulated by
the u.s department of transportation or the dot the benefits urine testing generally provides a
longer history of drug use than oral fluid testing the longer time window of detection built into the
process identifies risk and may therefore be preferred for risk-based programs the downside
it is not an impairment test and may not be permitted for certain types of non-dot-regulated
testing circumstances in canada as a consequence of certain court arbitration and human rights
commission decisions further urine testing is more susceptible to adulteration than is oral fluid or
hair testing for lab-based oral fluid testing the sample is collected using a swab and is shipped
to the laboratory for testing many clients use this for post-incident or post-accident
reasonable cause and random testing depending on the positive test cutoff levels analysis of
this sample type may indicate the likelihood of drug use within hours prior to the collection
and therefore could potentially indicate the likelihood of impairment during or in proximity to
the work shift every test is directly observed so there is less risk of adulteration or substitution
it is less invasive than urine testing and the dot is considering this test type for approval
but likely using longer time windows of use cutoff levels that will detect risk rather than
the likelihood of impairment the disadvantage of using test cutoff levels that reflect the
likelihood of very recent drug use is that for risk-based programs it does not provide a long
history of drug use meaning the identification of some intermittent or recreational drug users
may be missed by using this testing method and as stated before a positive result may only indicate
that the employee was likely impaired on the job there are no guarantees for urine point-of-care
testing the sample is essentially collected the same way as a lab-based urine collection but using
a container with built-in analytical capabilities the sample in this case is tested or screened
immediately on site thereby eliminating the time needed to ship negative screening test specimens
to the lab for analysis that means it provides an initial screening test result within five minutes
the screening test cutoff levels match those used for lab-based testing for the standard five panel
and poct kits can be considered reliable screening tools depending on company philosophy
unfortunately though a urine poct screen cannot be used to confirm a positive result
a lab confirmation test is required if the poct screen test is non-negative also the poct is
not as accurate as lab-based testing so there is a higher risk of false positives and false negatives
when comparing to the screening technology at the lab though the technology has proven more reliable
than oral fluid poct this test type is not yet approved by the dot for its regulated testing
program and there are no industry standard cutoff levels for the drugs tested for beyond
those included in the dot's standard 5 panel with oral fluid point of care testing the sample is
collected the same way as the lab-based oral fluid tests but using a device capable of immediate
screening on-site the test shows the screening result within 15 minutes of the collection
and every test is directly observed so there is less risk of adulteration the
disadvantage is that the poct test is an initial screening technology only and in itself is not as
accurate as initial screening technology used for lab-based testing as with urine poct non-negative
oral fluid poct results must be sent to a lab for confirmation testing and there's a greater chance
of false negatives or false positives compared to lab-based screening tests as well as currently
available urine poct tests the other downside is that studies show these kits appear to have
difficulty detecting drug use for some common drugs most notably marijuana at this time we do
not recommend the use of oral fluid poct testing due to the disadvantages we noted however we

hair testing involves cutting a segment of hair from the head or body and submitting
the specimen to a lab for analysis it is most commonly used by organizations that require
abstinence and risk-based drug testing programs this is a valuable test
because the standard one and a half inches of hair can provide a 90-day history of drug use
because of the longer detection time window and the fact that this collection is directly observed
the specimen cannot easily be compromised drug users cannot substitute or tamper with the sample

not an impairment test and may not be permitted for certain types of non-dot-regulated testing circumstances in canada as a consequence of certain court arbitration and human rights commission decisions further urine testing is more susceptible to adulteration than is oral fluid or hair testing for lab-based oral fluid testing the sample is collected using a swab and is shipped to the laboratory for testing many clients use this for post-incident or post-accident reasonable cause and random testing depending on the positive test cutoff levels analysis of this sample type may indicate the likelihood of drug use within hours prior to the collection and therefore could potentially indicate the likelihood of impairment during or in proximity to the work shift every test is directly observed so there is less risk of adulteration or substitution it is less invasive than urine testing and the dot is considering this test type for approval but likely using longer time windows of use cutoff levels that will detect risk rather than the likelihood of impairment the disadvantage of using test cutoff levels that reflect the likelihood of very recent drug use is that for metadata.title: When Is a DOT Drug Test Required? Post-Accident, Random, Reasonable Suspicion and More
metadata.author: Trucking Comply
metadata.shortDescription:
When must a DOT drug or alcohol test happen? This video walks through all six required tests: pre-employment (a verified negative and a Clearinghouse query before any safety-sensitive work), post-accident (when a death, an injury or a tow-away triggers a test, the citation windows, and the 2, 8 and 32-hour clocks), random (the 50 and 10 percent minimums, equal chance, unannounced tests spread through the year, and going to the test site immediately), reasonable suspicion (what a trained supervisor must observe and write down), and the return-to-duty and follow-up tests after a violation.

It is one module of Trucking Comply's FMCSA Drug and Alcohol Testing course. Every rule on screen is cited to 49 CFR Part 382 or Part 40, read on eCFR.

General information, not legal advice for your situation.

Chapters
0:00 Introduction
0:22 Pre-employment
2:13 Post-accident
4:59 Random
7:09 Reasonable suspicion
9:25 Return-to-duty
10:02 Follow-up
10:28 Recap
11:20 Take the course

Take the full course: FMCSA Drug and Alcohol Testing: https://www.truckingcomply.com/courses/fmcsa-drug-alcohol-testing?utm_source=youtube&utm_medium=social&utm_campaign=training-drug-alcohol-c3
The required tests (Part 382, Subpart C) on eCFR: https://www.ecfr.gov/current/title-49/subtitle-B/chapter-III/subchapter-B/part-382/subpart-C
Return-to-duty and follow-up testing (Part 40, Subpart O) on eCFR: https://www.ecfr.gov/current/title-49/subtitle-A/part-40/subpart-O

Trucking Comply — Keeping you in control, on and off the roads.

#DOTCompliance #FMCSA #Trucking
keywords: when is a DOT drug test required

segments.text: In this video,
we'll look at the six situations in which the DOT rules require a drug
or alcohol test, and the clocks and conditions that come with each one.
They are pre-employment, post-accident, random, reasonable suspicion,
return-to-duty, and follow-up, and we'll take them in that order.
The first test happens before a new driver does any safety-sensitive work.
The employer must have the driver's verified negative drug test result in hand
first, so a specimen that's been collected,
or a result that's still pending, isn't enough.
That result has to come from the medical review officer,
or from a consortium or third-party administrator, known as a C/TPA.
A lab printout the applicant brings in doesn't count.
The rule covers any driver the employer intends to hire or use,
so it applies to a leased owner-operator or an
occasional driver as well as to an employee.
The test has a twin. Before that first safety-sensitive work,
the employer must also run a full pre-employment query of the Clearinghouse,
which needs the driver's consent.
There's a narrow exception.
An employer can skip the pre-employment drug test only if the driver was in a drug
testing program under these rules within the last 30 days,
was tested within the past 6 months or was in a random pool for the past 12,
and has no known violation in the past 6 months.
Using the exception means getting written proof of all of that
from the driver's testing program, and keeping it on file.
An employer that uses a driver more than once a year without
employing them must get that proof again at least every 6 months.
An employer may also give a pre-employment alcohol test, but it doesn't have to.
One that does must test every new driver the same way, only after a job offer,
and must see a result under 0.04 before safety-sensitive work begins.
The second test follows a crash involving a truck on a public road.
Whether a test is required depends on what happened,
and on whether the truck's driver received a citation.
When someone dies,
the employer must test each of its surviving drivers who was doing
safety-sensitive work on that truck, for both alcohol and drugs.
A citation doesn't matter, and neither does who was at fault.
When someone is injured and immediately receives medical treatment away from the
scene, or a vehicle is so damaged it has to be towed away,
the employer tests only if the truck's driver
is cited for a moving violation from the crash.
The citation must come within 8 hours of the crash for the alcohol test,
and within 32 hours for the drug test.
A citation given only to the other driver doesn't trigger a test.
And the damage in a tow-away crash has a precise meaning.
The rule calls it disabling damage,
which is damage that stops a vehicle from leaving the scene in its usual way,
in daylight, after simple repairs.
Damage still counts as disabling if the vehicle could have been driven,
but driving it would have damaged it further.
A flat tire on its own, or a broken light, doesn't count.
Every required test must happen as soon as practicable, and three clocks apply.
If the alcohol test hasn't happened within 2 hours, the employer writes down why.
At 8 hours, it stops trying and records why.
For the drug test, it stops at 32 hours, and records why as well.
Meanwhile, a driver who must take a post-accident alcohol test may not drink for
8 hours after the crash, or until the test, whichever comes first.
The driver must stay available for the test, or may be treated as refusing it.
But medical care for anyone hurt always comes first,
and the driver may leave the scene to get help.
Because there's no time to look up the rules at the scene,
the employer must give drivers these post-accident instructions
before they ever drive, for example as a card kept in the cab.
A police breath or blood test for alcohol, or a police urine test for drugs,
can count,
if it meets the testing rules that apply to it and the employer gets the result.
And the rule doesn't apply to an incident that only involves
getting on or off a parked vehicle, or loading and unloading cargo.
The third test is random, and it runs all year with no event to trigger it.
Each year, an employer must test at least 50 percent of its average number
of driver positions for drugs, and 10 percent for alcohol.
FMCSA can change those minimums,
and it publishes any change in the Federal Register before the year it applies.
The selection must use a scientifically valid method,
such as a computer's random number generator,
and every driver must have an equal chance each time.
So the same driver can be picked twice in a row.
A selected driver must be tested during that selection period,
so a vacation doesn't take them off the list.
Random tests must be unannounced, and spread reasonably through the year,
not saved up for the last few weeks.
Only drivers covered by the rules may be in the pool, and all of them must be.
An employer may have a C/TPA make the selections,
with its drivers in a larger combined pool,
but the employer must make sure the C/TPA tests at the right rate,
with only covered drivers in the pool.
A driver covered by more than one DOT agency's rules at the same employer is
tested at the rate of the agency that regulates more than half of their work.
And an employer under more than one agency may keep a separate pool for each rate,
or one pool at the highest rate.
When a driver is told they've been selected, they go to the test site immediately.
A driver doing safety-sensitive work other than driving,
such as unloading, stops that work and goes as soon as possible.
Not showing up within a reasonable time after
being told counts as a refusal to test.
A random alcohol test can only happen just before,
during, or just after the driver's safety-sensitive work.
Random drug tests have no such limit.
The fourth test starts with what a person sees.
An employer must test when it has reasonable suspicion that a driver has broken the
alcohol or drug rules, and that suspicion must rest on specific, contemporaneous,
articulable observations of the driver's appearance, behavior, speech or body odor.
That means named signs, seen at the time, that can be written down.
For drugs, the signs can include the effects of long-term use and of withdrawal.
A tip, a rumor or a hunch isn't reasonable suspicion.
The observations must be made by a supervisor or company official trained
in the signs, with at least 60 minutes on alcohol and another 60 on drugs.
And the person who decides on an alcohol test doesn't conduct it.
An alcohol test for reasonable suspicion has its own time limits.
It's allowed only when the signs are seen during,
just before or just after the part of the working
day when the driver must follow these rules.
And like a random alcohol test, it can only happen just before,
during or just after safety-sensitive work.
Its clocks are the same as after a crash, but they start from the decision to test.
If the test hasn't happened within 2 hours, the employer records why,
and at 8 hours it stops trying and records why.
Even without a test,
a driver reasonably suspected of alcohol misuse can't do safety-sensitive work
until a test shows less than 0.02,
or until 24 hours have passed since that decision.
Beyond that, without an alcohol test,
the federal rule doesn't let the employer act against the driver based only on how
they look and behave,
though an employer may still act under its own company policy, within the law.
The supervisor must write down what they saw and sign it within 24 hours of
seeing it, or before the test results are released, if that comes first.
The last two tests are different.
They exist only for drivers coming back from a violation.
Both follow the return-to-duty process in Part 40, the DOT's testing procedures.
The return-to-duty test can only happen after the substance abuse professional,
or SAP, has found that the driver has successfully completed
the education or treatment they prescribed.
The result must be negative, and for alcohol, under 0.02,
before the driver goes back to safety-sensitive work.
Then come follow-up tests, unannounced, on a plan the SAP sets.
The plan must include at least 6 tests in the first 12 months back,
and it can run for up to 5 years.
Return-to-duty and follow-up drug tests are directly observed.
And follow-up tests come on top of random testing:
a random test doesn't count toward the plan.
To sum up, a new driver needs a verified negative drug test,
unless the narrow exception applies,
and a Clearinghouse query before any safety-sensitive work.
After a crash, a death means a test whether or not anyone is cited,
while an injury treated away from the scene, or a tow-away,
means a test only when the truck's driver is cited.
Random tests are unannounced and spread through the year,
and a selected driver goes to the test site without delay.
Reasonable suspicion needs a trained supervisor's specific observations,
written down.
And a driver returning from a violation takes a return-to-duty test,
then at least 6 follow-up tests in the first year back,
and those drug tests are directly observed.
This video is part of Trucking Comply's FMCSA Drug and Alcohol Testing course.
To take the full course, visit the page shown on screen.

metadata.title: DOT Drug Test Collection Procedure: What Drivers Can Expect
metadata.author: Green Spring US_Zero
metadata.shortDescription:
DOT drug test collection procedure explained from a driver’s point of view—see what happens from check-in to lab handoff.

Learn how identification checks, specimen handling, tamper-evident seals, and custody paperwork help protect your sample’s identity and integrity. You’ll also hear what you’re responsible for as the driver and when to ask the collector for clarification.

This educational video is part of ONE Mobile Drug Testing’s Drug Testing Explained series for CDL drivers, employers, and HR professionals.

0:00 What the collection process protects
0:16 Check-in and identification
0:35 Providing your urine specimen
0:49 Specimen checks, bottles, and seals
1:32 Your role as the driver
1:51 Laboratory handoff

Follow ONE Mobile Drug Testing for more straightforward drug testing explainers.
#DOTDrugTesting #CDLDrivers #UrineDrugTest #DrugTesting

segments.text: What happens after you arrive for a DOT
urine drug test? The DOT drug test
collection procedure is a series of
steps designed to identify your specimen
correctly and protect it from the moment
it's collected. Here's what to expect
from [music] check-in through handoff to
the laboratory. First, you'll provide
identification and the testing
information requested.
The collector will check the details and
explain what to do. The collector is
responsible for completing the required
collection procedures and paperwork.
Your part is to follow the instructions,
ask if anything is unclear, and provide
the required information. Next, you'll
be directed to the designated area to
provide your urine specimen. Follow the
collector's instructions about the
collection container and returning the
specimen. The goal is to keep the sample
secure and connected to the correct
test. Once you've handed it back, the
collector checks that it meets the
collection requirements. Then the
specimen is prepared for transport. In a
standard DOT urine collection, [music]
the sample is divided between the
required bottles, which are closed and
secured with tamper-evident seals. You
may be asked to initial the seals in
review or sign applicable paperwork.
Those steps help confirm that the
bottles are sealed and that the
collection record is complete. There's a
reason for each check. The collector
compares identifying information,
secures the specimen, and documents its
handling. Together, the identifiers,
seals, and custody paperwork help
[music] link the specimen to your test
and show how it was handled before it
reaches the laboratory. So as the
driver, remember three things.
Follow the collector's instructions,
check the information you're asked to
review, and speak up if something is
unclear. You don't need to manage the
collection paperwork yourself, but you
do have a role in confirming the details
required of you. And what's the next
step after the handoff? The secured
specimen and its documentation are sent
through the required process for
laboratory testing. The DOT drug test
collection procedure may feel formal,
but each step supports specimen identity
and integrity from collection through
processing.

metadata.title: How to Handle NEMT Cancelations
metadata.author: LearnCargo
metadata.shortDescription:
Dealing with last-minute cancellations is one of the toughest parts of running a non-emergency medical transportation (NEMT) business. In this video, we break down what really happens when clients cancel, why brokers often don't notify drivers in time, and the steps you must take to protect your schedule and get paid for your miles.

Key topics covered: • Why dispatchers and brokers fail to notify drivers • How to educate clients about canceling trips early • Steps to take with your broker after driving out to a canceled pickup • Protecting your route planning and daily revenue
